title: Is he mad? (Mark 3:20–30)
hook: his family think he's lost his mind; scribes say he's possessed
tomorrow: who are my mother and brothers?

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve names, called up into the hills. The word was apostle, one who is sent, and your line was first, to be with him. Who did your list of twelve include? Day one hundred sixty-nine.

Have you ever had your family worry about you in a way that stung? You changed jobs, or moved, or got serious about something, and someone at the kitchen table said, carefully, are you okay? Is this a phase? That's where Jesus is. He comes home, and the crowd is so thick nobody can even eat. And his own people hear about it and set out to bring him home by force. Mark doesn't soften what they said. And while they're on the road, important visitors arrive from Jerusalem with a darker explanation. Today: is he mad?
screen: `TOO BUSY TO EAT.` → `HIS OWN PEOPLE COME FOR HIM.` → `VISITORS FROM JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, they went to lay hold on him, "for they said, He is beside himself." Beside himself: out of his mind. The Greek word is the root of our word ecstasy, standing outside yourself. It's a startling thing for a gospel to include, that the people who knew Jesus longest thought he'd lost it. Then the scribes from Jerusalem go further. He's not mad, they say. He's possessed. He drives out demons by the power of the prince of demons, Beelzebul. Jesus doesn't shout. He calls them over and tells them parables. How can Satan cast out Satan? "And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand." If the powers of evil were fighting themselves, they'd be finished already. Then a picture: nobody can rob a strong man's house unless he ties up the strong man first. Christians hear Jesus saying that's what he's doing: tying up evil and taking back what it stole. Then comes a hard saying about the one sin that won't be forgiven, speaking against the Holy Spirit, and Mark explains it right away: they said he had an unclean spirit. Many Christians understand it as calling God's good work evil, so stubbornly that you can't turn back, and teachers often reassure worried people that fearing you've done it is a sign you haven't. And here's the line that traveled. In 1858 Abraham Lincoln borrowed it for a speech about a nation half slave and half free: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Mark's story is also a sandwich. Family sets out, scribes accuse, and tomorrow the family arrives.
screen: `HE IS BESIDE HIMSELF.` · `THE SCRIBES SAY: POSSESSED.` · `A HOUSE DIVIDED CANNOT STAND.` · `LINCOLN BORROWED THE LINE IN 1858.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with being misunderstood. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind a time someone got you wrong. Not a stranger. Someone close, who should have known better. Let yourself feel it for a moment: the sting, the wish to explain. Now notice that you don't have to win that argument in the next two minutes. You can let it be unfinished. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is. If not, just let it sit beside you without fighting it. The bell holds the time.
Is he mad? What his own people wondered, and what the scribes answered with something worse. Mark tells it without flinching.

Your line: a house divided can't stand. Today, notice one place where you're fighting yourself, saying one thing and doing another, and take one step to bring the two together. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

screen: `DAY 169 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO ARE MY MOTHER AND BROTHERS?`

howItsDone: Christians often turn to this passage when they feel misunderstood by family or friends for their faith, and many churches teach the strong-man picture as Jesus's victory over evil.

myth: the gospel hides that his family doubted him
Mark says it outright: his own people went to lay hold on him, saying he is beside himself.
a house divided cannot stand was first said by Abraham Lincoln
Lincoln borrowed it in 1858 from Jesus's words in the gospels.
the Greek word for beside himself is the root of ecstasy

fork.setup: you're Jesus. important visitors say, in front of the crowd, that you work by the power of the devil. what do you do?
options: call them over and answer with parables.
ask the crowd to throw them out.
fork.reveal: he calls them to him and answers in parables: how can Satan cast out Satan? a house divided cannot stand.

original.note: Greek: he stood outside himself, he's out of his mind. The same root gives English ecstasy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a house divided is a line from American history.
what it means: Jesus answers the charge that he's in league with evil: a kingdom or a house at war with itself can't last.
what a scholar hears: exeste, he stood outside himself. and Mark sandwiches the scribes' charge between his family setting out and arriving.

notes: KJV 3:21 has 'his friends' (Greek hoi par' autou, 'those belonging to him'); rendered as 'his own people' and 'family' given 3:31. Confirm.
ἐξέστη (from existēmi) and the link to 'ecstasy' (ekstasis); confirm.
The unforgivable sin (3:28–30) is treated briefly with a common pastoral reading ('fearing you've done it is a sign you haven't'); Keepers should confirm this is broadly acceptable across churches.
Lincoln's House Divided speech, Springfield, June 16, 1858; paraphrased. Confirm.
Beelzebul (Greek Beelzeboul; KJV 'Beelzebub'); confirm spelling choice.
